https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: Ray, the commander of Ukraine’s ninth ‘Kairos’ Battalion, an elite long-and-medium-range strike drone unit. ‘I feel revenge and a sense of justice,’ he says of his aerial attacks on Russia. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Ray, the commander of Ukraine’s ninth ‘Kairos’ Battalion, an elite long-and-medium-range strike drone unit. ‘I feel revenge and a sense of justice,’ he says of his aerial attacks on Russia. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian The Sunday read Ukraine ‘This is where democracy beats totalitarianism’: Ukraine’s drone strike force takes the fight to Russia Exclusive: At a launch site in the Ukrainian countryside, members of the elite ‘Magyar’s Birds’ brigade are turning Russia’s vast size into a weakness Luke Harding in Ukraine; photographs and video by Alessio Mamo Sun 2 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 01.01 EDT Share Sparrows were cheeping as the sun set over a field of tall yellow sunflowers when a moped-like growl suddenly disturbed the evening calm. The noise rose, dipped, and rose again. Lt Col Ray – a Ukrainian commander with the 414th aviation brigade – took cover in a leafy ditch. Seconds later a Ukrainian drone roared into a mauve sky. It jerked upwards at a 45-degree angle, orange flames fizzing, and then motored serenely onwards. The flying object resembled a sleek grey biplane with a wooden propeller and tail. It left behind clouds of billowing black smoke and a whiff of gunpowder. Four and a half years after Vladimir Putin sent tanks to seize Kyiv, the war in Ukraine has moved from the earth to the sky, turning into a battle of drones. This contest – unprecedented in the history of warfare – features technology, innovation and rapid development. “We are making history here. This is where democracy beats totalitarianism. It’s like George Orwell. But this time Big Brother loses,” Ray said, as the drone vanished over the horizon, engine thrumming. Its destination was Crimea, a scenic Ukrainian peninsula of beaches and white chalk mountains, stolen by Russia in 2014, and militarised thereafter. View image in fullscreen The launch of an Ukrainian FP1 long-range drone towards Russian-occupied Crimea. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian Next, two more long-range drones hurtled forward. They soared into the twilight, above a darkening steppe landscape. Each carried 50-100kg of explosives. Mission over, the Ukrainian soldiers packed briskly, winding up white cables with practised ease. Within 10 minutes the men were gone. They disappeared down a tree-lined and potholed track. Far away from the frontline, other crews were crisscrossing Ukraine, releasing drones according to a precise evening schedule. Operators sitting in front of computer screens nudged them towards enemy targets. The model can fly more than 2,500km, far enough to pummel anywhere in European Russia, and much of Siberia as well. The journey made by Ray’s trio of drones was shorter. After four hours, at about 1am, the first reached its endpoint: the holiday resort of Alushta on the southern coast of occupied Crimea. The drone weaved between grey apartment blocks and crashed into a 110kV electricity substation. Flames erupted, pricking the city’s inky blackness. View image in fullscreen A Ukrainian drone hits an electricity substation in Alushta. The 414th Separate Unmanned Strike Aviation Brigade, AKA Magyar’s Birds, hit 12 other power plants in occupied Crimea and southern Ukraine on the same night. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian These remote strikes on 21 July were part of what Ukraine has nicknamed the Crimean “switch off”: a campaign to disconnect the region from its power and logistics networks. The same night, unmanned drones hit 13 electricity nodes. Several were located in the Russian-controlled parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces, which the Kremlin says it has annexed. Since 2022 Russia has carried out nightly attacks on Ukrainian cities and towns. It sends Iranian-designed shaheeds as well as ballistic and hypersonic missiles. After Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, these swarms grew. They rain down chaotically, killing families in their apartments and other civilians, in a calculated campaign of terror. Once a recipient of western assistance, Ukraine has responded by developing its own military manufacturing base. After rapid growth, the country has become the world’s leading unmanned systems power. The drones hurled last week at Crimea were built in Kyiv by a defence technology startup. The firm’s representatives take part in operations. View image in fullscreen A Ukrainian FP1 long-range drone on its way to Russian-occupied Crimea. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian Ray’s battalion – named after Kairos, the ancient Greek god of opportunity, luck and the fleeting moment – has carried out hundreds of deep strikes against Russia. Targets have included oil refineries, warehouses and munitions depots. It has also struck ports and harbours, as well as routes used for army logistics such as roads and railways. In 2026 Ukrainian drones have struck Moscow and Putin’s home city of St Petersburg, embarrassing Russia’s president and bringing the war home to ordinary citizens who have previously ignored it. “I think Putin is afraid,” Ray suggested. “One of the justifications he gave for his war was to stop Ukraine from [potentially] bombing Moscow. It’s happening now as a direct consequence of his actions.” Ukraine long-range drone – loop Ray said he felt “revenge and justice” every time one of his drones ascended into the moonlit heavens, bound for enemy territory. “We didn’t start this war. We have no choice. We are fighting for our independence, for our people, for the memory of those who have died, and for our future. This is a contest between slaves and free people,” he said. Secrecy surrounds Ukraine’s well-organised drone operation. An analytics department finds targets. Western partners provide some intelligence, but most is open source. Drone crews are given coordinates at the last minute. So far none of those who take part in launches have been injured or killed, despite attempts by Moscow to identify and blow up lift-off points. One person involved said: “You are making change on a global scale. Trump wakes up and sees the results. At the same time it’s very solitary. You can’t tell anybody about what you do, even your wife, or boast: ‘Today we bombed Moscow.’ Only your commander understands.” They added: “It’s an important job. You feel the biggest satisfaction and a member of an elite.” Kairos is a part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces . In July Brovdi launched a campaign to destroy oil tankers and other vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea. So far, more than 200 have been hit. The Russians were taken unawares, their boats unable to escape. Since last week the brigade has been burning warehouses belonging to Wildberries , Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, obliterating at least nine of them. Ukraine says the company sells military products. The strikes have crippled small businesses and caused billions of roubles in damage. “The socio-psychological impact on society is greater than that of an oil refinery,” Brovdi said. View image in fullscreen Robert ‘Magyar’ Brovdi, the commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces. His 414th unmanned strike aviation brigade, known as Magyar’s Birds, has carried out a series of spectacular drone strikes on targets inside Russia. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian He said Ukrainian long-range drones had “significantly thinned out” Russia’s air defences. “We have already destroyed the majority of them,” he said. “With every air defence unit destroyed, the breach expands.” Three days earlier air defence units were flattened in the Russian port of Yeysk on the Azov Sea, he added, bringing the number of systems knocked out to 305. Russia’s enormous size – once a strategic strength – has turned into a weakness. A panicked Kremlin has moved “a certain number” of air defences from the frontline to protect Moscow, Brovdi said. The commander said he wanted to stop Russia from using Crimea as a “springboard” to fire on Ukraine and to push out the nearly 1 million Russian residents or “colonisers” who settled on the peninsula after Putin’s 2014 takeover. Crimea now has so little fuel that Russian military groups are sometimes unable to fill up and launch drones. There are also frequent power cuts. One brigade member, call sign Schweik, predicted food shortages would happen soon: “The operation is endless. There will be a cascade effect. We will continue this pressure. They will be thinking about survival instead of assault operations.” Schweik added: “The situation is humiliating for Russia. Crimea is symbolic. It was Putin’s first trophy and the place where the world order was broken. He created a kind of euphoria in Russia society, which in turn gave him permission to go and take more [Ukrainian] territory. Now everyone in the world understands that Russia is really weak.” Not all Ukrainian drones reach their targets. According to Ray, about a third are brought down over occupied territory. He admitted losses in the skies above Russia were considerably higher. Nevertheless, Ukraine’s strategy – to pile pressure on the Russian economy – appears to be working. “Troops and resources must be exhausted, so that it becomes impossible for them to continue the war,” Brovdi said. The commander acknowledged that Russian troops were still advancing in the eastern Donbas region, with battles in the city of Kostiantynivka. “Their gains to date do not justify the price they’re paying for them,” he said. He continued: “At this rate, with their intention to seize half of Ukraine, are they planning to fight for 100 years?” View image in fullscreen Panama, a senior sergeant with Ukraine’s ‘Kairos’ strike-drone battalion, says he has made peace with the summer’s swarming mosquitoes: ‘They are inhabitants of free Ukraine.’ Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian Back in the countryside, Ray’s colleague “Panama” described the latest launch as a success. “It was 10 out of 10. With us it’s always like this,” he said, adding that he had been working with the current biplane-like model for a year and a half. “To begin with we used foreign drones. Sometimes things went wrong. Now we don’t have problems,” he reflected. The only challenge came from the mosquitoes, which fill the air during summer evenings. “Over time we’ve become friends with them. They don’t annoy me any more. They are also inhabitants of free Ukraine. They can do whatever they want,” Panama said. “But if they irritate us we will launch them at the enemy. They can eat Russians.” Betrayal: Trump, Putin and The New Age of Conquest by Luke Harding is published on 27 August by Guardian Faber. Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/AP View image in fullscreen Russia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after an explosion outside a restaurant in central Moscow. Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Russia Head of drone manufacturer critically injured in car bomb in Russia Assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory Europe live – latest updates Pjotr Sauer Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.10 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The head of a leading Russian drone manufacturer has been critically injured in a car bomb near Ekaterinburg, in what appears to be the latest in a series of assassination attempts targeting figures linked to the country’s war in Ukraine. Vladimir Tkachuk, the founder of the private drone manufacturer Uraldronzavod, was rushed to intensive care on Wednesday after a bomb planted beneath his Mercedes exploded, according to Russian state media, citing emergency services. His bodyguard was killed in the explosion. The Russian news agency Tass reported that Tkachuk was in a critical condition and doctors were “fighting [to save] his life”. Images circulating on social media showed the charred wreckage of a Mercedes, with blood stains visible on the pavement nearby. Uraldronzavod is one of several private drone manufacturers that sprang up in Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine . The company is best known for producing the Upyr (Ghoul), a low-cost first-person-view (FPV) kamikaze drone manufactured using 3D-printing technology at its facility in Ekaterinburg and widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine. In 2024, Vladimir Putin visited the factory, where he was given a tour by Tkachuk. Uraldronzavod and Tkachuk have been hit with sanctions by western governments for their role in supporting Russia’s war. Tkachuk is also the founder of the popular pro-war Telegram channel Obsessed with War, which has more than 500,000 followers and has been used to raise funds and procure military equipment for Russian soldiers fighting on the frontline. Russia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after an explosion outside an upmarket restaurant in central Moscow that killed five people. Russian authorities have not identified the intended target of that attack, but pro-Kremlin bloggers and independent Russian media suggested it was aimed at Col Gen Aleksandr Chayko, the commander of Russia’s aerospace forces, who was reportedly celebrating his birthday at the restaurant. Among those killed was Chayko’s son-in-law Daniil Peredrya, the independent outlet Agentstvo reported on Wednesday, citing government records. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials, accusing them of involvement in war crimes. Ukrainian intelligence services have previously employed a range of tactics in operations inside Russia, including planting explosive devices beneath vehicles that can be detonated remotely. The latest assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue its clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory, and is likely to intensify scrutiny of Russia’s internal security apparatus and its inability to protect senior officials and pro-war figures. Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/Getty Images New South Wales NSW police settle trespass case after visiting Indigenous children’s home 150 times in 20 months Trespass case launched by two mothers settled after officers often went to families’ houses between midnight and 4am Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Fri 11 Sep 2026 00.51 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 01.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Indigenous mothers have settled a trespass case against New South Wales police, after officers turned up at one of their homes 150 times in 20 months to conduct bail checks on her sons. The case, which was launched against NSW police in April 2024, was settled on confidential terms three weeks before it was to go to trial in the supreme court. One of the complainants, a single mum who uses the pseudonym Megan for privacy, has two sons, who were on bail from the ages of 11 and 13 after being found as passengers in a stolen car. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Police attended her home in regional NSW more than 150 times over 20 months, with many of the visits taking place between midnight and 4am. NSW legislation allows courts to authorise police to attend a private residence to check that someone is complying with their bail conditions. But the Justice and Equity Centre, representing Megan in court, argued that many of the bail checks were done without court authorisation, which amounted to trespass. Megan said the visits often involved police banging on doors, shining torches through the windows and letting themselves in through the back gate in the middle of the night. She said the visits were scary and stressful for her family and resulted in her kids missing school because of exhaustion. ‘‘My eldest is driving around with his head held high now, knowing police can’t just randomly pull him over,’’ Megan said. ‘‘But I know he’s still shaking in fear about what they could do. ‘‘They’ve already done the damage, and it will take a lot for my boys to start trusting police again.” ‘Staggering’: watchdog condemns police after Indigenous teenager on bus wrongfully arrested – then searched Read more The other complainant, a single mum of three who uses the pseudonym Joanne, said police visited her western Sydney home to do bail checks on her son more than 90 times in 18 months. She said in the space of a few hours, police conducted three such checks. “The checks often happened on school nights, which meant my youngest daughter was too tired to go to school in the morning,” she said. NSW police said the officers were acting lawfully when they conducted the bail compliance checks. A police spokesperson said such checks were an important tool for keeping the public safe and managing risks associated with letting people out of jail during an ongoing court process. But a report from the state’s Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, released in 2025, found police were stretching their authority and powers by relying on a weak legal principle to conduct bail compliance checks without court authorisation. The mothers’ solicitor, Kate Sinclair, said it was immensely brave for her clients to bring the case against the force. ‘‘They did it for their families and their communities and we respect their courage,’’ she said. Megan and her sons have separately taken NSW police to the federal court for racial discrimination, arguing that the boys were targeted because they are Aboriginal. That case is ongoing. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief BUDAPEST, HUNGARY ( Worthy News ) – A Hungarian television and radio presenter has been fired after failing to immediately cut off a live caller who suggested using a sniper to “eliminate” Prime Minister Péter Magyar, amid wider concerns over violent political rhetoric in Hungary. Presenter Nóra Palányi lost her job after the caller made the remarks during Tuesday’s Paláver phone-in program, jointly broadcast by HírTV and HírFM. The woman first suggested that 300 to 400 “true Hungarians” should go to parliament and “clean out” politicians from Magyar’s Tisza Party — “but not with a broom” — according to Hungarian media accounts of the broadcast. Christian news. Biblical insight. Prayer alerts. Get the Worthy Brief by email. She then asked why Hungary did not have a “sniper” or a “good marksman” who could “eliminate” Magyar, while also saying she did not have murderous intentions. Palányi attempted at points to calm the caller but did not immediately terminate the conversation when the violent remarks were made. PRESENTER FIRED Mediaworks, which owns HírTV and HírFM, said Palányi had committed an “extremely serious professional error” by failing to immediately interrupt the caller despite established protocol and by distancing herself from the remarks only later. The company terminated her employment and launched an internal investigation aimed at preventing similar incidents. It also apologized to viewers, listeners and others affected. The controversy adds to scrutiny surrounding Paláver and HírTV’s treatment of Magyar. In April 2025, HírTV published corrections acknowledging that it had falsely reported several claims about Magyar’s alleged conduct toward underage girls at Budapest’s Ötkert nightclub. The broadcaster acknowledged that it had falsely reported, among other claims, that Magyar made obscene propositions to underage girls and threatened the father of one of them. One of the corrected reports was specifically associated with Paláver. EARLIER CONTROVERSY There is no indication that the earlier reporting controversy and Tuesday’s live caller were directly connected. The latest incident comes as Hungarian authorities and media organizations confront the consequences of increasingly confrontational political rhetoric in the country’s highly polarized public environment. It also emerged during another turbulent week for Hungary’s political and media establishment. Police confirmed that a former state secretary had been questioned as a suspect over alleged misuse of personal data following the massive leak of information from Tisza’s mobile application. Mediaworks had previously been fined 50 million forints, about $157,000, by Hungary’s data-protection authority after three of its publications linked to an interactive map containing personal information obtained from the Tisza data leak. The map exposed information connected to nearly 200,000 people. Separately, prosecutors announced another major development Thursday in a corruption investigation involving state-owned bus operator Volánbusz, saying five people had now been questioned as suspects over passenger-transport contracts and bus procurements. CORRUPTION PROBE Investigators allege that state-owned Volán companies suffered losses of around 10 billion forints, or about $31.4 million, between 2015 and 2018 through allegedly overpriced purchases of more than 600 used buses and other transactions. Prosecutors said suspected illegal payments in the case reached hundreds of millions of forints and, involving two suspects, billions of forints — equivalent to millions of dollars. Hungarian billionaire businessman Dániel Jellinek and Norbert Szivek, the former chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management Company, were among those detained. A Budapest court Thursday ordered them held for one month pending the investigation, although their lawyers appealed the decision. The court proceedings do not establish guilt, and Jellinek’s Indotek Group rejected the allegations against him, saying he had cooperated with authorities and committed no crime. The cases are not directly connected, but their emergence within days of each other has intensified scrutiny of Hungary’s political, media and institutional landscape as authorities claim to pursue several high-profile investigations. Photograph: Narendra Modi/YouTube View image in fullscreen Smit Machchhar, who is recovering in a hospital in Abu Dhabi, spoke to Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, in a video call broadcast live on television. Photograph: Narendra Modi/YouTube Flydubai plane incident ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up then ‘passengers would lose their lives’ Associated Press Fri 2 Oct 2026 04.39 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 04.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight has described how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent. Capt Smit Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, told the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, in a video call broadcast live on television news channels that he knew he had to get back on his feet to save the passengers onboard. “I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” he said on Friday from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives,” he told Modi. Machchhar, who is from Mumbai, was seriously injured in Wednesday’s attack but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and restrain the attacker as the Boeing 737 descended sharply, witnesses and Israeli authorities said. He has been hailed as a hero for his actions, with world leaders saying he helped prevent a potential disaster. The flight, carrying 182 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said the attacker, an Omani national, was arrested in Saudi Arabia and was undergoing interrogation there. His motive for the attack remains unclear. Machchhar said that during the difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage. “Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” he told Modi. Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for flydubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain. He logged more than 9,750 flying hours with SpiceJet. Composite: George Chidi/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Anti-Trump protesters, left; and Elliot Kim, the general manager of Suwanee Frame & Art. Composite: George Chidi/The Guardian US politics This Georgia county is one of the US’s most diverse – and that could flip multiple elections Gwinnett county is home to many immigrants and other newcomers, and how it votes could be decisive for Congress George Chidi Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Johanna Park might just be an ambassador for Gwinnett county, Georgia , one of the 10 most ethnically diverse counties in the United States. Park owns Cafe Amico at Suwanee Town Center, one of her three Italian coffee shops in the area just north of Atlanta. She was born in Korea and lived much of her life in Argentina and Peru. She’s been in Gwinnett for more than 20 years, part of an early wave of Korean immigration that’s built Korean American car dealerships, banks, insurance agencies, supermarkets and restaurants like her own. It’s also a population that’s increasing in influence and not just numbers . In 2020, Gwinnett was 30.6% white, 27.8% Black, 23.7% Hispanic, 13.2% Asian, and 4.0% multiracial, according to the US census. About 28% of Gwinnett residents were born outside of the United States. About half of those are US citizens. Extraordinary diversity is simply a fact of life here. According to the US census diversity index, there is an 84.9% chance that two randomly selected Gwinnett residents will belong to different racial or ethnic groups. Control of the Senate may come down to the results of Georgia’s contest between US senator Jon Ossoff and US congressman Mike Collins. And Georgia’s election may come down to a handful of places where turnout and partisan sentiment aren’t easily predicted. Gwinnett, with its surge in population, of both US-born newcomers and immigrants, may be one of those places. Park, who has generally voted for Democrats , has little good to say about the economy or the Trump administration. “They’re deporting all of the Hispanic people from here, left and right,” Park said. With little media fanfare, ICE began a “ shadow surge ” of arrests in August. Called “Operation Safe Community”, the agency detained more than 1,000 immigrants across metro Atlanta, disproportionately targeting immigrant-heavy communities along Buford Highway, Norcross and other parts of Gwinnett county. View image in fullscreen A resident and child walk near the Lawrenceville Lawn park in Lawrenceville. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images “And not only are they deporting them back to their country, but also they are deporting them to … to south[ern] Africa ? I don’t know where … And who’s paying for all of this? You know, probably you and I, with the tax money.” “Illegal immigration has always been a thing, but why are we are so adamant about kicking everybody out when they are the hardest working people here, and they help overall with the economy?” she asked. Park noted that Gwinnett’s immigrant community tends to be politically split between Republicans and Democrats. While the county fields more Asian American Democratic elected officials such as Akbar Ali in Lilburn, others such as Buford’s Soo Hong have been elected as Republicans. The idea of “Asian Americans” as a single voting bloc ignores nuances. Vietnamese American voters tend to be more Republican, while Indian American voters tend to be more Democratic. But neither party owns their loyalty. Park thinks this divide “will remain, always. It’s deeply rooted. Especially the business owners are mostly pro-Republicans because of the benefits and the tax cuts and what not.” Their children, however, may be another matter. They are often splitting with their parents, driven left with the broader trend of highly educated Americans siding with Democrats. Elliot Kim, general manager of Suwanee Frame & Art, said: “I’m Korean. My parents live here as well, and typically that generation of Koreans and maybe a little bit younger than them stay pretty Republican and conservative because they stay close to the church. That’s what they relate to. But myself and my brother probably lean a little bit more to the left.” Immigration has been one driver of the county’s explosive growth. Its extraordinary school system is another. US News and World Report ranked the Gwinnett School of Mathematics, Science and Technology as the top high school in Georgia and seventh nationally. It is also far and away the largest school district in Georgia, with more than 180,000 students . Even as public school enrollment falls across America, parents around Atlanta have been voting with their feet by moving to Gwinnett. That growth - not the war, not gas prices, not even Trump - might be the key political issue for Gwinnett voters. Though housing starts have fallen since the early 2000s boom, the county has been absorbing more than 10,000 new residents a year since. View image in fullscreen Voters cast their ballots in Gwinnett County in November 2024. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Take Suwanee, on the purple fault line between football-obsessed Buford near the Mall of Georgia to its north and Duluth, where the storefront signs alternate between English, Spanish and Korean, to its south. Kim, a graduate of Gwinnett’s vaunted public schools, is concerned that the school system today isn’t rigorous enough for his daughter, taking issue with how little homework is assigned and how often students are permitted to retake tests. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines US Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion “I mean the principal was going on and on about how Roberts [elementary school] is award-winning, best in state all this. And I’m like, how are these metrics even being formed here?” Kim said. “I am so unimpressed about what they’re learning, and maybe is that just me getting old and wanting my kids to have the amount of strife that I did going through school.” Thirty years ago, Suwanee’s town common was a cow pasture, a million-dollar home was a rumor and apartments were the punchline to a joke about Atlanta. Today, Suwanee’s town center is a model of suburban mixed-use development ringed with condominiums, and local property values are closer to Boston’s than Atlanta’s. Its population has increased fivefold since 1996. “My neighborhood is kind of in a bubble, I’m just going to say,” said Kristina Lindsey, a Democratic activist from Suwanee. “We have money. And so our neighborhood is not as concerned with what’s happening to maybe some people in southern Gwinnett, right? Or the gas prices or our grocery prices, right? … It does not affect us the same way it does someone who’s living paycheck to paycheck and doesn’t have an emergency fund.” She stood on the green at Suwanee with a group of about 20 people waving anti-Trump protest signs at a weekly demonstration. “I feel a moral obligation to be out here to be visible,” Lindsey said. “And so that other people who might share the same values as me see that we have the courage to be out here and make some noise.” For all of America’s focus on Georgia’s swing voters with the US Senate on the line, Gwinnett Democrats may be more motivated to flip control of the state legislature. Republicans have control of Georgia’s house chamber by a 10-vote margin. Gerrymandering protects some Republicans, but the vulnerable seats are in places like Gwinnett. Republican Matt Reeves represents part of Suwanee, along with some points north. He held on to his state house seat in 2024 by 621 votes on 29,003 ballots cast, and faces a rematch against Michelle Kang, an attorney and Korean American immigrant. There is little Republican red meat, culture war fodder, in his rhetoric. He talks about affordability – property tax relief, lowering insurance prices, and pushing for a statewide referendum for senior homestead tax exemptions. “Here’s the thing in Gwinnett county: we are the battleground. We have competitive seats,” Reeves said. “So I’ve brought my A-game every day for the last two years. And I’ve been saying affordability for at least the last two years, probably even before that, and I’m glad that the national conversation has caught up with that because we’ve got to deliver savings, for our people to have more money in their pocket.” State senator Adrienne White Carden heard much the same from voters as she knocked on doors. The longstanding Democratic political activist is married to a Gwinnett county commissioner and no stranger to retail campaigning. She won a special election by a 51-49 margin earlier this year in Gwinnett, serving in a temporary role until January. “I think people are still definitely concerned about the shenanigans that Trump is running, but at the same time, they’re more interested in what’s happening here at home,” Carden said. “You know, costs definitely came up, whether it be gas pump prices or, to be honest, as the wife of a county commissioner, those who knew I was his wife – which was many people – always had a message for Commissioner Kirkland Carden about property taxes.” Explore more on these topics US politics Georgia Jon Ossoff US Congress US Senate House of Representatives Democrats news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/19/russ.text: Russia has introduced visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens as part of a broader effort to deal with the collapse of Western visits since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with visitors from Asia and the Middle East.The number of tourists from EU countries travelling to Russia fell to around 160,000 in 2025, from just over 5 million in 2019. Cancelled direct flights, payment card restrictions and sanctions have effectively severed leisure travel from Europe and the US, and inbound tourism as a whole declined further in the first half of 2026.The Vietnam visa-free decree signed by Vladimir Putin and taking effect on Thursday covers tourists, businesspeople, members of delegations and transit passengers.Vietnamese nationals seeking long-term residency, employment or study in Russia will still require a visa. For several years, Russian citizens have been able to enter Vietnam visa-free for stays of up to 45 days.Vietnamese visitors to Russia rose 69% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to the Association of Tour Operators of Russia, which projects a further 25-30% increase after the visa requirement was removed.Vietnam has become the third most popular foreign destination for Russian travellers. Figures were also rising on the other end: the Vietnam National Administration of Tourism recorded 1,134,000 Russian visitors in the first nine months of 2026, a 160% increase, making Russia its third-largest source market.The visa arrangement followed an early September meeting in Moscow between Putin and Vietnamese President To Lam, who described the Russian leader as "a great friend and close brother of the Vietnamese people."Moscow and Beijing introduced reciprocal visa-free travel in late 2025, with Chinese arrivals growing but falling short of official expectations.The Russian government has projected 4.2 million Chinese visitors by year-end and 5.5 million in 2027. Up to 516,000 Chinese tourists arrived in the first half of 2026, a pace analysts described as well below those targets.Safety concerns have been cited as a factor, with reports of drone incidents over Moscow's airports attracting attention in Chinese media.Vietnam has not joined Western sanctions against Russia over the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and does not supply weapons to Kyiv. Hanoi has called for a ceasefire and negotiations but has avoided publicly criticising the Kremlin. China maintains a similar position of official neutrality.Russian government figures could not be independently verified.

Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images View image in fullscreen The peculiar circumstances of the discovery of Hunter Biden’s laptop raised concerns about the possibility of Russian disinformation. Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images FBI Two ex-FBI officials charged with lying about investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop Contents of laptop of Joe Biden’s son were part of a bizarre saga in the final weeks of 2020 presidential election Associated Press Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two former FBI intelligence officials who specialized in foreign election interference were charged on Friday with making false statements about their roles in investigating the origins of Hunter Biden ’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election . Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides surrendered on Friday and made their first appearance in federal court in Washington DC. Floris’s legal team expressed outrage at the development coming from the US Department of Justice, the parent agency of the FBI . “Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the [justice department] has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” her attorneys said in a statement. Trump appointee overseeing election investigations steps down from FBI role Read more The case was filed 10 days before the 3 November midterm elections and marks the latest in a series of high-profile and politically charged investigative actions the justice department has undertaken in the run-up during the height of campaigning ahead of the vote. The prosecution, a rare justice department criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and bizarre saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race, in which Joe Biden, Hunter Biden’s father, beat Donald Trump but Trump refused to accept the result and tried numerous ways to overturn it – which ended up in his second impeachment , accused of inciting an insurrection attempt on 6 January 2021 , and criminal charges that were ultimately dismissed after Trump’s 2024 election victory. Friday’s court proceedings also came amid a broader, backward-looking effort by the FBI director, Kash Patel , who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated Trump’s conservative base. The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump and Biden. The laptop’s contents were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop. The laptop contained emails that appeared to show discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings. The peculiar circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian disinformation, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community was assessing that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump’s behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.
